candidate.educational_objective: Explain that acute-care MRSA colonization is an indication for Contact Precautions and that CDC does not specify one universal discontinuation criterion; follow the facility infection-prevention policy.

options.A: Contact Precautions should stop automatically after 24 hours without fever because duration depends only on systemic symptoms and not on persistent colonization or transmission risk.
options.B: A single negative nasal culture is a universal national criterion for stopping Contact Precautions because one test reliably confirms permanent clearance of MRSA carriage.
options.C: CDC recommends Contact Precautions for MRSA in acute care, but no national recommendation defines a universal point for discontinuation; the facility’s infection-prevention policy should guide removal.
options.D: Colonization without infection never requires Contact Precautions in acute care because CDC limits this intervention to clients with active MRSA disease and draining wounds.

candidate.rationale: CDC recommends Contact Precautions in inpatient acute-care settings for patients colonized or infected with MRSA. In its MDRO recommendations, CDC states that no recommendation can be made regarding when to discontinue Contact Precautions because the issue is unresolved. Therefore, removal should follow the facility’s infection-prevention policy rather than a universal fever-free period or a single negative culture.
candidate.source_claim_supported: CDC recommends Contact Precautions for MRSA-colonized or infected acute-care inpatients and does not provide a universal discontinuation point for MDRO Contact Precautions.

candidate.stem: An acute-care inpatient is colonized with MRSA and is on Contact Precautions. The family asks when the precautions can be stopped. Which explanation is most accurate?
